claims.text: Introducing a controlled nanoscale dispersion of Y2O3 nanoparticles into a refractory high-entropy alloy will improve its radiation tolerance.
The Y2O3 dispersion will preserve the alloy's mechanical integrity under plasma-facing conditions.
Controlled powder-metallurgy processing can produce a uniform nanoscale Y2O3 dispersion in the alloy.
The intended structural state consists of nanoscale Y2O3 particles distributed within the alloy matrix and at grain boundaries.
Y2O3 nanoparticles act as sinks for irradiation-induced point defects.
Point-defect capture by Y2O3 nanoparticles promotes vacancy-interstitial recombination.
The Y2O3 dispersion mitigates the formation and growth of irradiation-induced defect clusters.
Mitigating defect-cluster formation and growth reduces accumulated irradiation damage.
The proposed benefit is expected under high-dose neutron or ion irradiation at approximately 500°C to 900°C.
The Y2O3-dispersed alloy will have a lower radiation-induced defect density than the unmodified alloy.
The Y2O3-dispersed alloy will exhibit less irradiation-induced swelling than the unmodified alloy.
The Y2O3-dispersed alloy will exhibit less irradiation-induced hardening than the unmodified alloy.
After irradiation, the modified alloy will retain yield strength within approximately 10% of baseline values.
After irradiation, the modified alloy will retain ductility within approximately 10% of baseline values.
Unmodified refractory high-entropy alloys typically exhibit greater irradiation-induced defect accumulation.
Unmodified refractory high-entropy alloys typically undergo mechanical degradation under irradiation.
The beneficial effect depends on the Y2O3 nanoparticles remaining stably dispersed without coarsening or agglomeration.
Nanoparticle coarsening or agglomeration at very high dose or outside the specified temperature range may compromise the benefit.
The magnitude of defect reduction and mechanical-property retention depends on nanoparticle volume fraction and processing parameters.
